clue.text: Desire a short time after church for conversation

indicators.note: after places the desire-and-time pieces behind the church abbreviation

parts.note: an itch is a restless craving or desire
T is the abbreviation for time, so time cut short

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a brief spell after the church service to have a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' tells you the church abbreviation CH comes first, with ITCH, A and T following it.
explanation.definitionFit: Light, idle talk or gossip is a casual kind of conversation.

clue.text: Words in the paper that may contribute to furrowed brow

definitions.meaning: the title printed in large type above a newspaper story
a wrinkle across the forehead, a line on the head

explanation.surface: A worrying news story makes a reader frown.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's big-type title, and literally a crease on the forehead that helps make a frown.

clue.text: Hunt met — folly, daft, everything you'd expect!

indicators.note: daft means crazy, so the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A fox hunt meets with every sort of foolishness one could imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daft' signals an anagram of HUNT MET plus FOLLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom meaning the whole lot, all that could be wanted.

clue.text: A cover hidden by explosive chemical

indicators.note: hidden by means the explosive abbreviation wraps round A and the cover

parts.note: HE stands for high explosive
a lid is a cover for a pot or box

explanation.surface: A lid is concealed by a bomb containing a dangerous chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hidden by' looks like a hidden-word signal, but here it is a container: the explosive abbreviation wraps round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A compound of a halogen such as chlorine or bromine with another element.

clue.text: Old city partially destroyed

indicators.note: partially means only part of the word destroyed supplies the answer, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: An ancient city was partly destroyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partially' points to the letters sitting inside DESTROYED.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient city of Homer's Iliad, besieged by the Greeks.

clue.text: Cover for the Christmas period?

parts.note: reads like a stand-in worker during the holidays, but is the decorative paper around presents

explanation.surface: Someone asks who will cover shifts over the Christmas holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative paper used to cover presents, the cover most used at Christmas.

clue.text: Country maiden attached to boxer

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over, one with no runs scored
Muhammad Ali, the famous heavyweight boxer

explanation.surface: A country girl is engaged to a boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attached to' just links M and ALI; M for maiden is cricket shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlocked West African nation, capital Bamako.

clue.text: Double the drink set down before the optimist or the pessimist?

definitions.text: Double the drink set down before the optimist or the pessimist?

parts.words: Double the drink set down before the optimist or the pessimist
parts.note: the optimist sees a vessel half full and the pessimist half empty; doubling that half-measure gives a complete measure

explanation.surface: A barman serves a double to two people with opposite outlooks.
explanation.definitionFit: The amount a drinking vessel holds when filled to the brim, twice a half measure.

clue.text: Artist during autumn depicting effect of clouds

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the crossword's usual artist
during means in, as in 'in the morning'
fall is the American word for autumn

explanation.surface: A painter at work in autumn captures how clouds look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' supplies its synonym rather than acting as a container signal, and autumn is given its American name.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain dropping from clouds is precipitation, the result they produce.

clue.text: Infant born west of Lincoln

indicators.note: in an across answer, west of means to the left of, so the born letter comes first

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for born in genealogies
Abe is the familiar name of Abraham Lincoln

explanation.surface: A baby is born in a place just west of the city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' looks like the English city but is US president Abraham (Abe) Lincoln; 'west of' puts B to the left in an across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A small baby or young child is called by this affectionate word.

clue.text: Reasonable, yes? Not English politicians concocting implausible tales!

parts.note: fair means reasonable, as in a fair price

indicators.note: Not tells you to leave the English letter out of the word yes

parts.note: the word yes, taken as written before the removal
Tories are members of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is fair that non-English politicians are inventing far-fetched tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not English' strips E from YES, leaving YS. TORIES are British Conservative politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanciful narratives full of magic and make-believe are the classic far-fetched stories.

clue.text: Dicky sent me parcel with new spare parts maybe

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the letters of sent me parcel are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poorly packed parcel arrives containing new spare parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' (British slang for shaky or unreliable, as in a dicky heart) signals an anagram of SENT ME PARCEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh components fitted to substitute for worn ones are substitutes; spare parts are one example.

clue.text: It's most stupid and evil interrupting short rest

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into the middle of the shortened nap word
short tells you to cut the last letter from the word for a rest

parts.note: a siesta is an afternoon rest
ill can mean evil, as in ill deeds or ill will

explanation.surface: Wickedness breaking into a brief nap is the most foolish thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims the final A from the nap word, giving SIEST; 'interrupting' then breaks into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A superlative of foolish: the most absurd or daft of all.

clue.text: Book to get your teeth into endlessly

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is cut from the word for chomping

parts.note: to bite is to get your teeth into something

explanation.surface: A book you can really sink your teeth into, one that never seems to end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' trims BITE to BIT. The book is from the Apocrypha of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of the Apocrypha telling of a pious Israelite in exile in Nineveh.

clue.text: Last message of female cheating

parts.note: RIP, rest in peace, is the final message on a gravestone
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman's final message reveals that she was being unfaithful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last message' is RIP, the words carved on a tombstone; the definition is a noun, a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindle or fraud is a piece of cheating that overcharges or dupes someone.

clue.text: Channel island statue

definitions.meaning: one of the small Channel Islands, near Guernsey
a square stone pillar topped by a carved head

explanation.surface: A statue stands on an island in the English Channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny Channel Islands isle off Guernsey, and an ancient Greek pillar sculpture bearing a bust.

clue.text: Book that's right bad, awful, covered by journalist

indicators.note: covered by means the journalist word wraps round the right letter and the rearranged bad

parts.note: a hack is a jobbing journalist

indicators.note: awful suggests the letters of bad are put in a mess

explanation.surface: A journalist covers up a truly terrible book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' scrambles the three letters of bad; the right letter plus that scramble goes inside the journalist word, signalled by 'covered by'.
explanation.definitionFit: A volume bound in stiff boards rather than a paper cover.

clue.text: Jazz that's live — British work

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
op, short for opus, is a work of music

explanation.surface: Someone praises live jazz as a fine British creation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'live' is the verb to exist, giving BE; 'work' is OP, short for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast, complex style of 1940s jazz associated with Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie.

clue.text: Two pubs, mostly very cold and uncivilised

indicators.note: Two means the pub word is written twice in a row

parts.note: a bar is a pub, or a room in one

indicators.note: mostly means the word for very cold loses its final letter

parts.note: icy means very cold

explanation.surface: A pub crawl in freezing weather turns uncivilised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two pubs' gives BAR twice; 'mostly' cuts ICY to IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Savage and cruel, as of tribes outside civilisation.

clue.text: Be sick having swallowed new dye

indicators.note: having swallowed means the sickness word takes the new letter inside it

parts.note: to ail is to be ill or sick

explanation.surface: Someone falls ill after swallowing a fresh dye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having swallowed' puts N inside AIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo, the blue colouring obtained from a West Indian shrub, goes by this name.

clue.text: One sadly misled having absorbed a philosophical theory

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: having absorbed means the rearranged letters take in the article a
sadly suggests the letters of misled have gone wrong and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A person sadly led astray has taken in a philosophical idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges the six letters of misled into DELISM; 'having absorbed' puts the article inside it after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Any doctrine holding that reality is fundamentally mental or spiritual, as in Berkeley or Hegel.

clue.text: Predecessor of policeman gets smuggler

definitions.meaning: the Bow Street force in eighteenth-century London came before the modern police
one who brings contraband in illegally, as in gun- or rum-

explanation.surface: A police forerunner arrests a smuggler.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bow Street officers were London's early law enforcers, and a contraband carrier is called a gun- or rum- one.

clue.text: Carrying mammal, Edward moved unsteadily

indicators.note: Carrying means the Edward nickname holds the mammal inside it

parts.note: Ted is a short form of Edward
an otter is an aquatic mammal

explanation.surface: Edward staggered about while carrying an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrying' makes Edward's pet name the container; the surface reads as Edward carrying an animal, which is exactly the mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: To walk with a shaky, wobbling gait as if about to fall.

clue.text: Dealer putting up crimson paintings?

indicators.note: in a down answer, putting up means writing the pieces bottom to top

parts.note: crimson is a shade of red
paintings are works of art

explanation.surface: A dealer hangs crimson pictures on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting up' turns RED plus ART upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant who buys and sells goods for profit.

clue.text: Sort of communication that could come from bad guy with an ogle

indicators.note: could come from means the letters of the following words are rearranged to produce the answer

explanation.surface: A villain leering at someone sends a message without words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could come from' signals an anagram of BAD GUY plus AN OGLE; 'with' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Gestures, posture and facial expression convey meaning without speech.

clue.text: Animal cherished from what we hear

indicators.note: from what we hear says the word is identified by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: dear means cherished or beloved

explanation.surface: A beloved creature, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from what we hear' signals that DEAR (cherished) sounds like the animal's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoofed ruminant such as the stag or the roe, with antlers.

clue.text: Fellow participating in smashing entertainment

indicators.note: participating in means the answer takes part in, sits within, the words smashing entertainment

explanation.surface: A man joins in a fantastic show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'participating in' points to letters spanning the end of SMASHING and the start of ENTERTAINMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A man, short for gentleman.

clue.text: Fix 18 when half confused

indicators.note: half confused means only the front half of the word from 18 is turned around

parts.note: 18 across is the dye word, taken from its grid answer

explanation.surface: Something at 18 is repaired when partly muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 across is ANIL; 'half confused' swaps its first half AN to NA.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten or secure something in place, as with a metal spike.

clue.text: Artefact that's frightfully nice art? Nothing in it!

indicators.note: in means the nothing letter goes inside the rearranged letters
frightfully suggests the letters of nice art are thrown into disorder

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at pleasant art, saying there is nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frightfully' rearranges NICE ART into CREATIN; 'in' puts O inside it before the final N.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made or produced by an artist or craftsman is a work they have made.

clue.text: Four notes out of order? That's irritating!

parts.note: ti is a note of the sol-fa scale
re is a note of the sol-fa scale
so is a note of the sol-fa scale
me (mi) is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone hears four notes played in the wrong order and finds it annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: The four sol-fa notes TI, RE, SO and ME are 'out of order' because they are not in scale sequence; the phrase is a hint, not an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Annoying or tedious, wearing on one's patience.
